Religion wasn't the biggest cause. It was nationalism. People felt personally offended like you had pissed on their mother if you insulted their country.

They thought it was reasonable to engage in fisticuffs over a remark about french cheese's supposed inferiority, or a remark about the alleged silliness of German soldiers' hats.

People celebrated the start of WWI because they were finally going to avenge the many insults against their great nation. WWII was started partly to avenge the humiliation of Germany.

Because of new and more destructive weaponry, the death toll of total war was much higher than before, which made it far more scary than it ever had been. After two rounds of that madness, the value of national honour got downgraded a lot.

Second to that, the great powers from before WWI ended up being either completely dismantled, or much weaker. After WWII they lost the vast majority of their colonies, being unable to enforce their authority.

Politicians worked hard to create an environment where total war was no longer an intention, much less an option. The whole point of the EEC (which later became the EU) was to promise to never do total war again, and to create mutually beneficial economic ties to make total war a rather bad idea in practical terms, too.

The rise of secularism is not a very big factor, but it certainly helps remove one excuse for carpet-bombing our neighbours.

Ultimately, Latin grammar is fairly simple -- there are a few basics, and after that it's just rote memorization. The real issues come when you start reading real Latin (not the synthetic stuff in learning texts). Latin has some peculiar idioms to it, and more often then not writers will break grammatical rules.

The real issues with that Latin site are that: * It focuses on translating English to Latin, whereas people starting out should focus on translating Latin to English. * Some of the translations it provides are just plain wrong.
Wheelock's Latin will work if you have a solid grasp of grammar and some familiarity with any of the romance languages. Ecce Romani is more basic.
Thank you! They look wonderful~ Will I be able to get through these without a teacher? I'll take a look at the pair of them, anyway. edit: typo

If you've studied english or a foreign language intensively then you can probably manage. Wheelock's has a pretty extensive site: http://wheelockslatin.com/. Just like traveling abroad, if you're making the effort people will be much more willing to help you out. Latin nerds will get tired of translating for you but are usually pretty willing to correct you if you've made an effort rather than just picking words out of a dictionary.
